Title: How often does a mixed type intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm on imaging indicate pathological involvement of the main pancreatic duct?
Text:
Original Article
How often does a mixed type intraductal papillary mucinous
neoplasm on imaging indicate pathological involvement of
the main pancreatic duct?
Kosuke Takahashi,1,3 Ichiro Yasuda,1
Toshiki Entani,1 Iori Motoo,1 Nobuhiko Hayashi,1
Takayuki Ando,1 Haruka Fujinami,1 Kazuto Tajiri,1 Johji Imura,2 Kenichi Hirabayashi,2
Eisuke Ozawa,3 Hisamitsu Miyaaki3 and Kazuhiko Nakao4
1Third Department of Internal Medicine,
2Diagnostic Pathology, Faculty of Medicine, Academic Assembly,
University of Toyama, Toyama, 3Department of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Nagasaki University Graduate
School of Biomedical Sciences and 4Department of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Sasebo City General
Hospital, Nagasaki, Japan
Objectives: A
pancreatic
cyst
>5 mm
in
diameter
that
communicates with the dilated main pancreatic duct (MPD)
≥5 mm on imaging is deﬁned as mixed type intraductal papillary
mucinous neoplasm (MX-IPMN). However, the frequency of
tumor involvement of the MPD in MX-IPMN remains unknown.
This study investigated how often MX-IPMNs involve the MPD
and whether MPD involvement can be diagnosed by peroral
pancreatoscopy (POPS).
Methods: This retrospective cohort study included patients
who underwent POPS for MX-IPMN followed by surgical
resection
between
July
2018
and
December
2021.
The
pathological features of MX-IPMN, including tumor extension
to the MPD, were analyzed. Additionally, the diagnostic
performance of various imaging modalities in detecting tumor
extension to the MPD was evaluated.
Results: Among a total of 15 patients, 10 (67%) had patholog-
ically conﬁrmed tumor extension to the MPD. In most cases with
pathologically conﬁrmed MPD involvement, the main tumor was
diagnosed as high-grade dysplasia (60%) or invasive carcinoma
(10%). Conversely, low-grade dysplasia was the main lesion in
most cases without MPD involvement (low-grade dysplasia 80%;
high-grade dysplasia 20%, invasive carcinoma 0%). The diagnostic
accuracy, sensitivity, and speciﬁcity of POPS with or without
biopsy was 93.3%, 90.0%, and 100%, respectively. POPS demon-
strated higher accuracy and sensitivity than computed tomogra-
phy,
magnetic
resonance
cholangiopancreatography,
and
endoscopic ultrasonography (accuracy: 93.3%, 40%, 60%, and
80%; sensitivity: 93.3%, 10%, 40%, and 70%, respectively).
Conclusions: Overall, 67% of MX-IPMNs had pathologically
proven MPD involvement. Tumor extension to the MPD is highly
suspicious of malignancy, and POPS may be useful for
evaluating MPD involvement.
Trial registration: The study was registered in the University
Hospital Medical Information Network clinical trials registry
(UMIN000051649).
Key
words: BD-IPMN,
ERCP,
IPMN,
single-operator

INTRODUCTION
M
ORPHOLOGICALLY,
INTRADUCTAL
PAPIL-
LARY mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) is divided into
two major categories: (i) main duct IPMN (MD-IPMN) and
mixed-type IPMN (MX-IPMN) that involve the MPD
and/or branch ducts, and (ii) branch-duct IPMN (BD-
IPMN) that only involves the peripheral pancreatic ducts.1
BD-IPMNs have a very low risk of cancer progression; in
contrast, MD- and MX-IPMNs often become cancerous.2,3
IPMNs involving the MPD are more aggressive and
generally require surgical treatment.2,4 This subdivision is
traditionally
based
on
the
imaging
characteristics
in
computed
tomography
(CT)
or
magnetic
resonance
imaging/cholangiography
(MRI/MRCP),
and
has
been
validated by morphological analysis of pancreatic resection
specimens.5–10 According to the International Consensus
Guidelines, cystic lesions of the branch duct with MPD
dilation ≥5 mm are diagnosed as MX-IPMN.11 However,
conﬁrming the presence of actual lesions within the MPD in
MX-IPMN
remains
challenging.
Since
2000,
peroral
pancreatoscopy (POPS) has made it possible to visually
inspect the target region and perform targeted tissue

sampling for morphological diagnosis of pancreatobiliary
diseases.12–18 However, the frequency of pathological
lesions within the MPD in clinically suspected cases of
MX-IPMN remains unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to
evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of imaging modalities,
including POPS, in detecting lesions within the MPD in
cases of MX-IPMN.
METHODS
Patients
W
E RETROSPECTIVELY REVIEWED the medical
records of patients who underwent POPS using the
SpyGlass-DS system (Boston Scientiﬁc, Natick, MA, USA)
for MX-IPMNs based on radiologic imaging at Toyama
University Hospital between July 2018 and December 2021.
POPS was performed when surgery was considered due to
high-risk stigmata, including MPD dilatation >10 mm or
enhancing mural nodules >5 mm, such as three phase
1 mm-slice enhanced CT, MRI/MRCP, or endoscopic
ultrasonography (EUS). The diameter of the MPD was
measured at the most dilated site on horizontal sections of the
CT images. MX-IPMNs were deﬁned as lesions meeting the
diagnostic criteria for both BD-IPMNs and MD-IPMNs.11
The study protocol was approved by the institutional
review board of our institution (R2020184) and registered in
the University Hospital Medical Information Network
clinical trials registry (UMIN000051649). All patients
provided informed consent for the procedure.
Procedure
All patients underwent EUS and ERCP under conscious
sedation with midazolam while their vital signs were being
monitored. EUS was performed using either a radial
scanning echoendoscope (GF-UE290; Olympus Medical
Systems, Tokyo, Japan) or curved linear echoendoscope
(GF-UCT260; Olympus Medical Systems) connected to an
ultrasound scanning system (EU-ME2; Olympus Medical
Systems). Contrast-enhanced imaging was used to distin-
guish nodular lesions from mucin in the cysts by observing
the blood supply to the lesions.
Pancreatography was performed in the prone position to
visualize the MPD and cysts. If the cyst was not visualized, the
junction between the cyst and MPD was estimated based on
other imaging modalities. For POPS, the SpyGlass-DS was
advanced through the 4.2 mm working channel of the
therapeutic duodenoscope (TJF-260 V; Olympus Medical
Systems) into the pancreatic duct. The contrast agent,
pancreatic juice, and mucin were aspirated before making
observations using the SpyGlass-DS. The type of protruding
lesion was classiﬁed into ﬁve types: granular (type 1), ﬁsh
egg-like without vascular images (type 2), ﬁsh egg-like with
vascular images (type 3), villous (type 4), and vegetative (type
5), as previously described by Hara et al.19 The irrigation
solution was collected for cytology. Cytological results were
graded into classes I through V. Targeted biopsy was
performed using SpyBite (Boston Scientiﬁc). When a
continuous MPD lesion extending from the target cystic
lesion was identiﬁed by POPS, a targeted biopsy was
performed for deﬁnitive pathological diagnosis. If no MPD
lesion was observed, biopsies were obtained from the junction
between the cyst and MPD. Additionally, negative biopsies
were performed to ensure accurate surgical planning. For
lesions located in the pancreatic head, negative biopsies were
obtained from the MPD at the junction of the pancreatic head
and body, and from a slightly more distal section of the MPD.
For lesions in the pancreatic body or tail, negative biopsies
were obtained from the MPD at the same junction and from a
slightly more proximal section of the MPD. Pathologically,
the lesions were classiﬁed as low-grade dysplasia (LGD),
high-grade dysplasia (HGD), and associated invasive carci-
noma (IC) according to the Verona consensus.20
Deﬁnitions
The following criteria were used to diagnose the presence of
MPD lesions in IPMN using CT, MRI, and EUS.
CT: intraductal extension of a mural nodule with contrast
enhancement within the MPD.
MRI: intraductal extension of a mural nodule within the
MPD on T2-weighted images.
EUS: intraductal extension of a mural nodule within the
MPD. Enhanced mural nodules within the MPD were
assessed using contrast-enhanced ﬁndings.
The diagnoses of MPD lesions on CT, MRI, EUS, and
POPS were independently and blindly reviewed by three
gastroenterologists specializing in the pancreaticobiliary ﬁeld
(I.Y., H.N., and T.K.). The ﬁnal interpretation of the imaging
ﬁndings was determined by a majority vote. In cases where the
three reviewers had differing opinions, a consensus was
reached through group discussion. For evaluating the
interobserver reliability, we used Fleiss’ j. A lesion was
deﬁned as malignant based on the following ﬁndings: (i) the
protruding lesion in the MPD was type 4 or 5; (ii) cytological
result was suspicious for malignancy or malignant; and (iii)
pathological result was HGD or IC. A lesion not meeting any
of the above criteria was deﬁned as “benign.”
The area of MPD involvement was deﬁned as follows: (i)
area where a lesion was detected in the MPD by CT, MRCP,
EUS, ERCP, or POPS; and (ii) area where a lesion was
detected by targeted biopsy.

The diagnosis of malignancy and area of MPD involve-

Statistical analyses
Continuous variables and categorical variables are presented
as medians (range) and as numbers (percentage), respec-
tively. Between-group comparisons were performed using
the Mann–Whitney U-test for continuous variables or the
v2-test for categorical data. Differences were considered
signiﬁcant when the P-value was less than 0.05. Interreader
agreement was determined by Fleiss’ j and interpreted by
the criteria of Landis and Koch.21 Interreader agreement
analysis was performed with R statistical software (version
3.5.1; R Foundation, Vienna, Austria). Other statistical
analyses were performed using JMP software (version
15.0.0; SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, NC, USA).
RESULTS
Baseline patient characteristics
D
URING THE STUDY period from July 2018 to
December
2021,
381
patients
with
suspected
BD-IPMN were referred to our hospital (Fig. 1). Among
them, 26 patients were diagnosed with MX-IPMN based on
CT, MRCP, and EUS. Of these, 15 patients who underwent
POPS and surgical resection at our hospital were analyzed in
this study.
The baseline characteristics of the 15 patients are shown
in Table 1. The patients included 11 men and four women,
with a median age of 72 years (range 61–83 years). Imaging
ﬁndings suggestive of MX-IPMN were incidentally detected
in 13 patients (87%). The median sizes (largest diameters) of
the cyst and MPD were 34.0 mm (range 19.0–56.0) and
10.0 mm (range 6.1–18.6), respectively. The main tumor
location was the pancreatic head in nine, body in three, tail
in one, head and body in one, and the whole pancreas in one
patient. MPD involvement was observed in one, four, and
seven patients by CT, MRI, and EUS, respectively. In all
cases, the proximal diameter of the MPD was dilated
≥5 mm. Consequently, the probability of reaching the
target
site
via
POPS
was
100%
(15/15).
Regarding
POPS-associated complications, mild pancreatitis occurred
in one case (7%), which resolved with conservative
treatment.

characteristics

in four, and total pancreatectomy in two patients. Among
the 15 surgical specimens, the ﬁnal histopathological
grading was LGD in seven, HGD in seven, and IC in one
patient. Ten of 15 (67%) patients were pathologically
proven to have lesions in the MPD.
The relationship between presence of MPD involvement
and pathological results is shown in Figure 2. MX-IPMN
with MPD involvement was observed in three (30%)
patients with LGD, six (60%) with HGD, and one (10%)
with IC. In contrast, most lesions without MPD involvement
were LGD (LGD 80% [4/5], HGD 20% [1/5], and IC 0%
[0/5]).
Detection of MPD involvement in MX-IPMNs
using imaging modalities
The diagnostic results for MPD involvement in MX-IPMNs
using various imaging modalities are shown in Table 3.
POPS without biopsy (visualization alone) had an accuracy,
sensitivity, speciﬁcity, positive predictive value, and nega-
tive predictive value of 93.3%, 90.0%, 100%, 100%, and
83.3%, respectively. The diagnostic accuracy was identical
between patients undergoing visualization alone and patients
with addition of biopsy during POPS. However, the
accuracy and sensitivity of POPS were higher compared to
those of CT, MRCP, and EUS (accuracy: 93.3% for POPS,
40% for CT, 60% for MRCP, and 80% for EUS; sensitivity:
93.3% for POPS, 10% for CT, 40% for MRCP, and 70% for
EUS). Table 4 shows the interreader agreement for detection
of MPD involvement using various imaging modalities.
Interreader agreement was weak for CT, whereas it was
almost perfect for MRI, EUS, and POPS (CT, j = 0.236;
MRI, j = 0.880; EUS, j = 1.000; POPS, j = 1.000).
MPD involvement in MX-IPMN was identiﬁed using CT,
MRI, and EUS in seven of 15 patients (Fig. 3). In two of the
remaining eight cases, MPD involvement was identiﬁed by
POPS. The ﬁnding of MPD involvement using all imaging
modalities was consistent with the postoperative patholog-
ical diagnosis.
Details of the imaging modalities and pathological
diagnoses of the primary lesion and MPD component in
all cases are summarized in Table 5. Among the eight cases
with carcinoma as the primary lesion, four (50%) showed
carcinoma within the MPD component. In cases 1 and 8,
MPD involvement was not identiﬁed on CT, MRI, or EUS.
However, POPS showed ﬂat lesions with ﬁsh egg-like
vascular patterns. Both cases were pathologically diagnosed
as intraductal papillary mucinous adenoma with MPD
components. Only in one case (case 13) was carcinoma
detected in the MPD component in the surgical specimen,
even though all imaging modalities, including POPS with
targeted biopsy, failed to conﬁrm MPD involvement.
Among all patients with MPD involvement based on CT,
MRI, or EUS ﬁndings, lesions were identiﬁed within the
MPD during POPS (Fig. 4).

Guidelines for IPMN management state that surgery should
be considered in patients with MPD dilatation of 5–9.9 mm
(a worrisome feature), presence of mural nodule(s) ≥5 mm,
positive cytology for malignancy, or main duct features
suspicious of malignant involvement.4 The evidence-based
European Guidelines also recommend surgical resection of
IPMN with MPD dilatation of 5–9.9 mm if the patient is ﬁt
and expected to have a long life expectancy.
In
this
study,
67%
(10/15)
of
MX-IPMNs
were
pathologically proven to have lesions in the MPD. Overall,
70% of MX-IPMNs with MPD involvement were malignant
(HGD 60%, IC 10%). Conversely, most lesions without
MPD involvement were benign (LGD 80%). Therefore,
MPD involvement may indicate malignancy in MX-IPMN.
A thorough evaluation of MPD involvement in MX-IPMN
is essential for the appropriate selection of patients for
surgery.
CT, MRI, and EUS are considered mandatory in the
assessment of IPMN, especially for evaluating mural
nodules4; however, it could be difﬁcult to detect MPD
involvement in MX-IPMN with these modalities. Although
POPS can potentially detect unexpected lesions not detected
by other imaging modalities, its usefulness for detecting
MPD involvement remains controversial. Arnelo et al.30

POPS. Moreover, we used Fleiss’ j to analyze intra- and
interobserver agreement among the three investigators in
interpreting each imaging modality. Intraobserver errors
in POPS, MRI, and EUS were assessed as “almost perfect
agreement” and unlikely to occur. However, interobserver
error in CT was assessed as “slight agreement.” Therefore,
POPS may contribute to improving the diagnostic accuracy
and reducing interobserver variability.
Nevertheless, targeted biopsy using POPS did not
improve the diagnostic accuracy compared to visualization
alone. The lack of improvement in diagnostic accuracy may
be attributed to limitations in the manipulation of biopsy
forceps and the use of a small cup. Furthermore, even
though an MPD lesion was not identiﬁed by POPS with
targeted biopsy in case 13, carcinoma was detected in the
MPD component of the surgical specimen, indicating a
limitation in the diagnostic performance of POPS. Addi-
tionally, POPS-related complications, particularly acute
pancreatitis and perforation, warrant close attention. The
incidence of pancreatitis reportedly ranges from 0% to
17%.32,33 To minimize the risk, careful and gentle scope
manipulation is essential.
However,
as
noted
previously,
POPS
can
identify
potentially malignant lesions in the MPD. If POPS shows
MPD involvement, surgery may be recommended. Con-
versely, if POPS does not show MPD involvement, the lesion
is likely to be LGD and may contribute to the discussion of
whether surgery should be avoided. Furthermore, POPS may
also be useful for assessing the extent of lesion extension to
determine the extent of resection.30 Thus, POPS may be
valuable in the preoperative diagnosis of MX-IPMN to
determine the extent of resection and need for surgery.
This study has some limitations. First, this was a
retrospective single-center study with a small sample size.
Therefore, large prospective studies are needed to validate
our ﬁndings. Second, although POPS is useful for direct

relatively large pancreatic ducts. Because the pancreatic
duct is very thin and has a complex branching structure, it
can sometimes be difﬁcult to insert the pancreatoscope
into all areas. Additionally, mucus or blood within the
pancreatic duct may obstruct the ﬁeld of view, making
comprehensive evaluation of the lesion difﬁcult. We tried
to remove the mucus and blood within the pancreatic duct
as much as possible for detailed valuation of MPD
involvement. Third, the diagnostic performance of POPS
in this study was not based on POPS alone but supported
by CT, MRI, and EUS as adjunctive diagnostic tools.
Moreover, the indication for POPS was determined based
on the presence of proximal MPD dilatation through
which a pancreatoscope could be passed, which may have
introduced selection bias.
In conclusion, 67% (10/15) of MX-IPMNs were patho-
logically proven to have lesions in the MPD. MPD
involvement may indicate malignancy in MX-IPMNs. POPS
is useful for the evaluation of MPD involvement that is
suggestive of malignancy.
